cards.title: pH vs pOH: −log of a base concentration is pOH, not pH

1_context.syllabus_hook: pH = −log[H+] and pOH = −log[OH−] (data booklet section 1); Kw = 1.00 × 10−14 at 298 K (section 2). pH + pOH = 14.00 follows from these but is not printed in the data booklet: memorise it.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach the formulas separately; exams hide the base inside an answer option so the reflex −log(c) is applied to [OH−].

trap_boundaries: A weak-base pH that comes out below 7 gets no error-carried-forward credit (25M.2.HL.6221.3).
Stopping at pOH when pH was asked is a recurring lost mark (24M.2.SL.TZ2.3).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Full marks need the conversion step written out: [OH−] → pOH → pH (or Kw/[OH−] → [H+] → pH).

disguises: 'Which solution has a pH of 9.0?' with base concentrations as options
3_novel_application.heuristic: Before any arithmetic, decide which side of 7 the answer must be on and which ion the concentration describes.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Calculate = working shown; a bare final value only scores if the markscheme says 'Award [n] for correct final answer'.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Once pH + pOH = 14.00 is memorised, you don't need to rebuild it from Kw each time.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 1 prints pH, pOH and Kw = [H+][OH−]; section 2 gives Kw's value. The shortcut pH + pOH = 14.00 is not printed: derive it from those two sections or memorise it.

rules: A strong base at 10^−n mol dm−3 (n ≤ 6) has pH = 14 − n; any option giving pH = n is the pOH trap.
At pH 4.50, [OH−] must be below 10^−7: eliminate 10^−4 and 10^−5 options instantly.
A base concentration of 10^−9 mol dm−3 cannot give pH 9: water's own ions dominate, so pH ≈ 7.

evidence.note: 45% correct; 24% chose the option that treats −log[base] as pH
no ECF if pH < 7 for a base

cards.title: Strength is extent of ionization, not number of protons or concentration

1_context.syllabus_hook: Strong and weak acids/bases differ in the extent of ionization.
1_context.textbook_gap: Diprotic and concentrated acids are often described as 'stronger' in everyday language; the exam rewards only the ionization argument.

trap_boundaries: Explanations based on the number of acidic protons are marked wrong (24M.2.HL.TZ1.1, 14M.3.SL.TZ2.21).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Name the property (extent of ionization) AND the comparison (strong: complete; weak: partial).

disguises: 'Why does sulfuric acid have a lower pH than methanoic acid of the same concentration?' with a 'diprotic' option
Two acids of equal concentration titrated with the same base
3_novel_application.heuristic: If the option is true but explains a different quantity (protons per molecule, solubility), it is a distractor.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Explain = reason + consequence: 'ionizes more completely, so [H+] is higher, so pH is lower'.

workflow: Spot equal concentrations in the stem
Ignore proton count unless moles are asked
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No calculation needed to rank equal-concentration acids by pH.

6_data_booklet.hack: pKa + pKb = 14 is printed in the data booklet, section 1.

rules: 'Diprotic' explains moles of base needed, not why the acid is strong: eliminate it on 'why lower pH' questions.
Equal moles of HCl and CH3COOH need the SAME volume of NaOH to neutralize: any option that says the strong acid needs more is out.
'More soluble' is never the reason an acid is strong.

evidence.note: 29% attributed lower pH to the acid being diprotic
number of acidic protons confused with strength
shifted the equivalence volume, confusing strength with concentration
few saw that the same volume of base is needed
same volume of acid needed was missed
